definition: The traditional narrative that recounts the origin of the world, of the gods, of rites or of cities, handed down without an assignable author and reinvented with each retelling. In Greek, *muthos* first means speech and story; it is opposed to *logos*, argued discourse, only from the philosophers and historians onwards, who class under this name what they want to hold at a distance. Xenophanes reproaches the poets for having lent the gods the vices of men; Plato drives Homer out of his city but invents his own myths; Aristotle distinguishes in the tradition a true core and mythical additions meant to persuade the multitude, the first political reading of myth, which the essay follows from Averroes to the Grand Inquisitor. In the twentieth century, Bultmann wants to demythologize the New Testament, Lévi-Strauss reads myths as systems of oppositions, Girard as the story of the lynching seen by the lynchers, and Blumenberg describes the work on myth as a way of holding at a distance the absolutism of reality. See also Allegory, Demythologization, Mythicist thesis.

In the Greek city, the offence done to the gods of the community: profaning a sanctuary, parodying mysteries, mutilating statues, teaching doctrines that turn people away from worship. Since Greek religion has neither dogma nor Church, impiety is not a heresy, an error of belief, but an attack on the civic order, judged by the ordinary courts. Anaxagoras had to leave Athens, Protagoras is said to have been prosecuted, and Socrates was condemned to death in 399 BCE for not recognizing the gods of the city and for corrupting the young. In Book X of the *Laws*, Plato makes it a doctrine: three impieties, denying the gods, believing them indifferent, believing that they can be bought with sacrifices, and a graduated punishment, from the house of correction to death for the repeat offender. The essay sees in it the pure case of its criterion, the first law that makes critique a crime in the name of an absolute. Christians will in their turn be accused of atheism for having refused the sacrifices. See also Sacrifice criterion.

The secret initiation rites of the Greek and Roman world, open to the individuals who chose them, alongside the public cults of the city: the mysteries of Eleusis, devoted to Demeter and Persephone, Orphism, then in the Hellenistic and Roman period the cults of Cybele and Attis, of Isis and Osiris, of Mithras. The initiate formed in them a personal relationship with a deity and often received the hope of a better fate after death; the secret was so well kept that what was shown there is poorly known. The history of religions school, with Bousset, explained part of Pauline Christianity by these cults, the title of Lord, baptism and the meal as initiations, and the mythicists saw in them the model of a Christ as a dying and rising god; historians have since strongly qualified these parallels. The essay encounters them in Plotinus, who compares union with the One to a mystery that cannot be divulged, and in the section on the existence of Jesus. See also Mythicist thesis.

The theatrical genre born in Athens in the sixth century BCE in the cult of Dionysus, performed at the civic festivals of the Dionysia before the whole city. Its three great authors, Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, take up the heroic myths, the Atreids, Oedipus, Antigone, the Bacchae, to stage conflicts without issue between the gods, the city, the family and the individual. Aristotle defines it by the imitation of an action which, through pity and fear, brings about the purification of these emotions. Hegel sees in it the collision of two equally legitimate rights, Nietzsche the union of the Apollonian and the Dionysian that Socrates supposedly killed, Vernant the moment when the city questions its own values. For Girard, tragedy is half lucid: it shows the symmetry of the adversaries that myth hides, and sometimes lets the victim's complaint be heard, but it ends by ratifying the expulsion. The essay encounters it in the Girard section and in the boxes devoted to Weil, to Sartre and to the Bacchae. See also Myth, Scapegoat mechanism.
